subject: physics
title: Measuring length and time
summary: Measure length accurately with a ruler and a vernier caliper, avoid parallax error, and time a pendulum in a way that reduces error.
objectives: Choose a suitable instrument to measure a length
Read a ruler and a vernier caliper correctly, avoiding parallax error
Time a pendulum using many oscillations and repeated readings
Calculate the period of a pendulum from timing data

sections.title: The right tool for the job
sections.body:
A tailor at Kamwala market uses a soft tape measure to measure your waist. A builder uses a long steel tape to mark out a house. A mechanic uses a vernier caliper to check the thickness of a brake disc. Each person picks a tool that suits the size of the object and how exact the answer must be.

The smallest division on an instrument tells you its precision. Precision means how finely the instrument can measure.
bullets: Tape measure: long lengths, like a classroom or a football pitch
Metre rule: lengths up to 1 m, marked in cm and mm
School ruler: short lengths, to the nearest 1 mm (0.1 cm)
Vernier caliper: small lengths and diameters, to the nearest 0.1 mm (0.01 cm)

sections.title: Reading a ruler or metre rule
sections.body:
The smallest division on a ruler or metre rule is 1 mm, which is 0.1 cm. So you record readings to one decimal place in cm, for example 12.4 cm.

The end of an old ruler is often worn or damaged, so the zero mark may not be exact. A good habit is to line up one end of the object with a clear mark, such as 1.0 cm, and then subtract.

Length = end reading − start reading.

sections.title: Worked example: using a ruler with a worn end
sections.problem: The left end of a pencil is lined up with the 1.0 cm mark. The right end is at the 13.4 cm mark. How long is the pencil?
steps: Step 1: Write down the start reading: 1.0 cm.
Step 2: Write down the end reading: 13.4 cm.
Step 3: Length = end reading − start reading = 13.4 cm − 1.0 cm = 12.4 cm.
sections.answer: The pencil is 12.4 cm (124 mm) long.

sections.title: Parallax error: where you put your eye matters
sections.body:
If you look at a scale from the side, the mark seems to move against the object behind it. You then read a value that is too high or too low. This is called parallax error.

To avoid it, put your eye directly above the mark, so your line of sight is at right angles (90°) to the scale. Keeping the ruler flat against the object also helps.

sections.question: Where should your eye be when you read the end of an object against a ruler?
options: A little to the left of the mark, so you can see more of the scale
Directly above the mark, looking straight down at the scale
A little to the right of the mark
It does not matter, as long as the ruler is long enough
sections.explanation: Your line of sight must be at 90° to the scale, directly above the mark. Looking from the left or the right makes the mark seem to shift, which is parallax error. The length of the ruler has nothing to do with parallax.

sections.title: The vernier caliper
sections.body:
A vernier caliper has two scales. The main scale is marked in cm and mm, like a ruler. The vernier scale slides along it. Its 10 divisions together are 9 mm long, so each one is 0.9 mm. This clever trick lets you read to 0.1 mm, which is 0.01 cm.

To read it: first, read the main scale at the line just to the left of the vernier zero. Next, find the one vernier line that lines up exactly with any main-scale line. That vernier line number tells you how many 0.01 cm to add.

Before measuring, close the jaws and check that the vernier zero lines up with the main-scale zero. If it does not, the instrument has a zero error that you must correct for.

sections.title: Worked example: reading a vernier caliper
sections.problem: A learner measures the diameter of a marble. The vernier zero is just past the 1.5 cm mark on the main scale, and vernier line 8 lines up exactly with a main-scale line. What is the diameter?
steps: Step 1: Main scale reading (just left of the vernier zero) = 1.5 cm.
Step 2: Vernier line that lines up = 8, so add 8 × 0.01 cm = 0.08 cm.
sections.answer: The diameter of the marble is 1.58 cm (15.8 mm).

sections.question: On a vernier caliper the main scale reads 3.5 cm and vernier line 6 lines up exactly. What is the reading?
sections.explanation: Reading = main scale + (vernier line × 0.01 cm) = 3.5 + 6 × 0.01 = 3.5 + 0.06 = 3.56 cm. 4.1 cm comes from adding 0.6 instead of 0.06. 3.65 cm mixes up the digits, and 3.506 cm uses 0.001 cm per line, which is too small.

sections.title: Measuring time with a pendulum
sections.body:
The SI unit of time is the second (s). In the laboratory we use a stopwatch. A digital stopwatch shows 0.01 s, but your hand is much slower than that. Your reaction time, the delay between seeing something and pressing the button, is about 0.2 s. This adds error at both start and stop.

A simple pendulum is a small heavy ball, called a bob, hanging on a string. One oscillation is one complete swing: from A, through B, to C, and back through B to A. The time for one oscillation is called the period (T).

To reduce error: time many oscillations (for example 20) and divide by 20. Repeat the timing a few times and take the average. Start and stop the watch as the bob passes the centre B, where it moves fastest and is easiest to judge.

sections.title: Worked example: finding the period of a pendulum
sections.problem: A learner times 20 oscillations of a pendulum three times. The readings are 32.1 s, 31.8 s and 32.1 s. Find the period.
steps: Step 1: Add the three readings: 32.1 + 31.8 + 32.1 = 96.0 s.
Step 2: Average time for 20 oscillations = 96.0 s ÷ 3 = 32.0 s.
Step 3: Period T = time for 20 oscillations ÷ 20 = 32.0 s ÷ 20 = 1.6 s.
Step 4: Why this helps: a 0.2 s reaction error is shared over 20 swings, so the error in T is only about 0.2 ÷ 20 = 0.01 s.
sections.answer: The period of the pendulum is 1.6 s.

sections.title: Common mistake: counting "one" when you start the stopwatch
sections.body:
Many learners say "one" as they press start. When they stop at "twenty", they have really timed only 19 oscillations, but they still divide by 20. The period comes out too small.

To avoid it, count "zero" as you start the watch, then "one" when the bob next passes the same point moving in the same direction. Stop the watch on "twenty".

sections.question: A pendulum makes 10 oscillations in 18.0 s. What is its period?
sections.explanation: Period = total time ÷ number of oscillations = 18.0 s ÷ 10 = 1.8 s. 0.56 s comes from dividing the wrong way round (10 ÷ 18). 180 s comes from multiplying, and 8.0 s comes from subtracting.

sections.title: Key points
bullets: Choose the instrument to suit the length: tape, metre rule, ruler (to 0.1 cm) or vernier caliper (to 0.01 cm).
Length = end reading − start reading. Do not trust a worn zero end.
Avoid parallax error: put your eye directly above the mark, at 90° to the scale.
Vernier reading = main scale reading + (line that lines up × 0.01 cm).
One oscillation is A → B → C → B → A. Time many oscillations, repeat, average, then divide to find the period.

quiz.question: What is the smallest division on a normal school ruler?
quiz.explanation: A school ruler is marked in millimetres, so its smallest division is 1 mm (0.1 cm). To measure to 0.1 mm you need a vernier caliper.

quiz.question: What causes parallax error when reading a scale?
options: The eye is not directly in line with the mark
The scale is marked in millimetres
quiz.explanation: Parallax error happens when you look at the scale at an angle, so the mark seems to shift against the object. Keep your eye directly above the mark, at 90° to the scale.

quiz.question: To what precision can a vernier caliper measure?
quiz.explanation: Each vernier division is 0.9 mm, 0.1 mm shorter than a main-scale division. This lets a vernier caliper read to 0.1 mm (0.01 cm), ten times finer than a ruler.

quiz.question: One end of a stick is at the 2.0 cm mark of a ruler and the other end is at 9.6 cm. How long is the stick?
quiz.explanation: Length = end reading − start reading = 9.6 − 2.0 = 7.6 cm. 9.6 cm forgets that the stick did not start at zero, and 11.6 cm adds the readings instead of subtracting.

quiz.question: The main scale of a vernier caliper reads 5.2 cm and vernier line 3 lines up exactly. What is the reading?
quiz.explanation: Reading = 5.2 + 3 × 0.01 = 5.2 + 0.03 = 5.23 cm. 5.5 cm comes from adding 0.3 instead of 0.03, and 8.2 cm comes from adding 3 whole centimetres.

quiz.question: A pendulum completes 20 oscillations in 36.0 s. What is its period?
quiz.explanation: Period = 36.0 s ÷ 20 = 1.8 s. 720 s comes from multiplying 36 × 20, and 0.56 s comes from dividing 20 ÷ 36, the wrong way round.

quiz.question: Why is it better to time 20 oscillations of a pendulum than just one?
options: The pendulum swings faster after many swings
The reaction-time error is shared over many swings, so the error in each period is much smaller
One swing is too fast for any stopwatch to record
Timing more swings makes the string longer
quiz.explanation: Your reaction time adds roughly the same error (about 0.2 s) however many swings you time. Spread over 20 swings, the error in one period is about 0.2 ÷ 20 = 0.01 s. The period of a pendulum does not change as it keeps swinging.

quiz.question: Three learners time 10 oscillations of the same pendulum and get 12.4 s, 12.6 s and 12.5 s. What value should they use for the time of 10 oscillations?
quiz.explanation: Take the average: (12.4 + 12.6 + 12.5) ÷ 3 = 37.5 ÷ 3 = 12.5 s. 37.5 s is only the total. Averaging repeated readings reduces the effect of random errors, giving a more reliable value.

glossary.definition: How finely an instrument can measure, shown by its smallest division.
A reading error caused by looking at a scale at an angle instead of straight on.
An instrument with a sliding vernier scale that measures small lengths to 0.01 cm (0.1 mm).
When an instrument does not read zero when it should, for example when the jaws of a caliper are closed.
One complete to-and-fro swing of a pendulum, from A to C and back to A.
The time taken for one complete oscillation, measured in seconds.
The short delay between seeing something happen and responding to it, such as pressing a stopwatch.
